source.note: Four rules written for this repository as format examples. They describe common camera grammar in my own words. Replace this file with your own library; do not commit a library you have no right to redistribute.

rules.title: Over-the-shoulder reverse
rules.purpose: Hold two speakers in one spatial relationship while the audience tracks who holds the floor.
rules.conditions: Two characters, seated or standing at a stable distance. Camera behind and slightly beside the listener's shoulder. Alternate sides only on a deliberate cut.
rules.risk: Swapping shoulders without a cut reads as a jump; the listener's shoulder can eat the speaker's face if the lens is too long.

rules.title: Low angle on approach
rules.purpose: Make an entering figure occupy more of the frame than their distance justifies, without dialogue.
rules.conditions: Camera below chest height, tilted up, subject walking toward lens. Keep the horizon out of frame or the tilt reads as a mistake.
rules.risk: The subject's feet leave frame and the walk loses contact with ground; a wide lens here turns the face into a caricature.

rules.title: Motivated push-in
rules.purpose: Convert a decision into a change of distance, so the audience feels the moment land.
rules.conditions: A visible trigger in frame: a hand closing, a head turn, a line finishing. Push starts after the trigger, not before.
rules.risk: Pushing without a trigger reads as drift; if the push outruns the subject's motion the model smears the face.

rules.title: Foreground reveal
rules.purpose: Introduce a third presence by moving the camera past something that was hiding it.
rules.conditions: A doorway, pillar, or shelf at the frame edge. Camera tracks laterally until the occluder clears the subject.
rules.risk: The occluder can clip through the subject mid-move; a reveal that lands too early spends the surprise before the cut.
